intro: The second conditional (If I had more time, I would travel) talks about imaginary, unlikely or untrue present situations and their results. We also use it to give advice and to speak politely.
objectifs: Build the second conditional with if + past simple and would + base verb.
Tell the difference between a real, likely situation (first conditional) and an imaginary or unlikely one (second conditional).
Use If I were you… to give advice, and were with every subject in careful English.
Vary the result with could and might, and ask hypothetical questions (What would you do if…?).

texte: Condition: if + past simple (or past continuous). Result: would + base verb. Contraction: 'd (I'd, she'd); negative: wouldn't. The comma rule is the same as in the first conditional.
The past tense here doesn't talk about the past: it shows distance from reality. “If I had a car” = I don't have a car (now).

lignes: we would see her more often.

sections.note: Like will, would never goes in the if-clause: “If I would have money” is wrong.

sections.titre: Real or imaginary? First or second conditional
texte: The choice depends on how the speaker sees the situation. First conditional: possible, realistic. Second conditional: imaginary, unlikely or impossible.
“If I win the match, I'll be happy” (I'm a good player; it's possible). “If I won the lottery, I'd stop working” (a dream; very unlikely).
exemples: If I get the job, I'll move to Lille.
If I got a job in Japan, I'd learn Japanese.
If I were taller, I'd play basketball.
Impossible to change: contrary to reality.
What would you do if you saw a lion in the street?

texte: With be, we can use were with every subject: If I were, if he were, if it were. This is the recommended form in writing and in exams. Was (if I was, if she was) is common in speech but less formal.
“If I were you, I'd…” is the classic way to give advice. In this fixed phrase, always use were.
exemples: If I were you, I'd apologise.
If it were cheaper, more people would buy it.
I wouldn't sign that contract if I were you.

texte: In the result, could = would be able to, might = would perhaps. In the condition, could = was able to: “If I could drive, I'd help you move.”
Hypothetical questions are very useful in conversation and in job interviews: What would you do if…? Where would you live if…? Short answer: Yes, I would. / No, I wouldn't.

lignes: If I had time, I would help you.
certain result in the imaginary situation
If I had a car, I could drive you home.
If you asked him nicely, he might say yes.
If I could speak Dutch, I'd apply for that job in Ghent.

texte: The second conditional makes a request or suggestion softer: “Would it be OK if I left early today?”, “It would be great if you could send me the file.” The grammatical distance creates polite distance.
It also helps to say no kindly (“I'd love to come, but…”) and to talk about principles (“I would never lie to a friend.”).
exemples: Would you mind if I opened the window?
It would be helpful if you arrived ten minutes early.

formule: If + past simple, would / could / might + base verb (If I had time, I'd help you. · If I were you, I'd…)
prononciation: 'd is almost silent: “I'd go” /aɪd ɡəʊ/. Listen for the small /d/ that separates “I go” from “I'd go”. Before a vowel it links: “I'd ask” /aɪˈdɑːsk/.
would is weak in questions: “What would you do?” /ˈwɒt wəd jə ˈduː/; often “wouldja” /ˈwʊdʒə/ in fast speech.
wouldn't /ˈwʊdnt/: the l is silent (as in could and should).
were is weak /wə/ in “If I were you”: /ɪf aɪ wə ˈjuː/, with the stress on you.
The voice rises on the condition and falls on the result, as in the first conditional.
erreurs: If I would have more time, I would travel.
If I had more time, I would travel.
No would in the if-clause: use the past simple.
If I had money, I will buy a car.
If I had money, I would buy a car.
Past simple in the condition → would in the result (not will).
If I am you, I would accept.
If I were you, I would accept.
Fixed phrase: If I were you.
If I would be rich, I would help my family.
If I were rich, I would help my family.
Be in the past (were) after if.
What you would do if you lost your job?
What would you do if you lost your job?
If I could, I would to help you.
If I could, I would help you.

dialogue.contexte: Abidjan, at a café terrace. Awa and her friend Pierre, visiting from Quebec City, imagine a different life.
lignes: What would you do if you didn't have to work?
I'd open a small restaurant by the sea. And you?
If I had the money, I'd travel around Africa for a year.
You could start with Ghana. It isn't far from here.
True. But if I left my job, my boss would be furious!
If I were you, I'd ask for unpaid leave.
Advice with If I were you.
That's a good idea. He might accept if I asked him early.
And if you came back next year, you could eat at my restaurant!
Second conditional for a friendly idea.

mots: imagine
Imagine you lived on an island.
to form a picture of something in your mind
afford
If I could afford it, I'd buy a bigger flat.
to have enough money to buy something
lottery
What would you do if you won the lottery?
a game where people buy tickets to win money
apologise
If I were you, I'd apologise.
to say sorry (US: apologize)
advice
Can I give you some advice?
an opinion about what someone should do (uncountable)
unpaid leave
She took unpaid leave to travel.
time away from work without pay
rather
I'd rather stay here.
would rather = would prefer
mind
Would you mind if I sat here?
to be annoyed or worried by something
dream
In my dream life, I'd live by the sea.
something you very much want; perfect, ideal

exercices.consigne: Choose the form that matches the meaning given.
items: (Possible) If it (rains / rained) tomorrow, we'll cancel the picnic.
rains
(Imaginary) If I (am / were) a bird, I'd fly to Cameroon.
were
(Imaginary) If she (has / had) wings, she would fly.
had
(Possible) If you (call / called) me tonight, I'll explain.
call

exercices.titre: 2. Put the verbs in the right form
exercices.consigne: Complete with the correct forms (second conditional).
items: If I ___ (know) her number, I ___ (call) her.
knew … would call ('d call)
We ___ (not / live) here if we ___ (have) a choice.
wouldn't live … had
If he ___ (be) more patient, he ___ (be) a good teacher.
were (was) … would be
What ___ you ___ (do) if you ___ (lose) your passport abroad?
would … do … lost
If they ___ (can) speak French, they ___ (move) to Quebec.
could … would move

exercices.consigne: Rewrite the sentence in the second conditional to imagine the opposite.
items: I don't have a car, so I can't drive you home.
If I had a car, I could drive you home.
She's very busy, so she doesn't call her parents.
If she weren't (wasn't) so busy, she would call her parents.
We don't speak Dutch, so we don't understand the signs.
If we spoke Dutch, we would understand the signs.
It's raining, so we aren't going to the beach.
If it weren't (wasn't) raining, we would go to the beach.

exercices.consigne: Each sentence has one mistake. Write it correctly.
items: If I would win the lottery, I would buy a house.
If I won the lottery, I would buy a house.
If I am you, I would talk to her.
If I were you, I would talk to her.
If she had time, she will help us.
If she had time, she would help us.
What you would say if he asked you?
What would you say if he asked you?

exercices.consigne: Write a second conditional sentence for each situation.
items: You don't have much time, but you'd love to learn the piano.
If I had more time, I would learn the piano.
Give a friend advice: don't say anything.
If I were you, I wouldn't say anything.
Ask a friend to imagine living in Brussels.
What would you do if you lived in Brussels?
Ask politely if you can leave earlier.
Would you mind if I left earlier?

exercices.consigne: Answer in 4 sentences: “What would you do if you could live anywhere in the world?” Use would, could and might.
items: Example answer

If I could live anywhere, I'd choose Vancouver. I would live near the mountains and go hiking every weekend. I could also work from home for a company in Europe. My family might visit me every summer.

a_retenir: If + past simple, would + base verb: an imaginary or unlikely situation (present or future).
The past tense shows distance from reality, not past time.
If I were you, I'd… to give advice; were is possible with every subject.
Could = would be able to; might = would perhaps.
